messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Jamal was 25, an African American journalist in a relationship, and when he first came to treatment he spoke in a controlled, careful way that made it clear how much effort it took him to keep his thoughts organized. He described himself as someone who had once been lively and enthusiastic, the kind of person who moved easily through deadlines, conversations, and crowded city streets, but now felt, in his words, “always miserable.” He said the trauma had not only frightened him in the moment but had destroyed the life he had known and taken away the version of himself that had defined him.

The event he returned to was an encounter with police that had turned terrifying without warning. He did not give every detail in one smooth account; when he tried, he lost the thread and had to stop, looking down and starting again. He explained that there had been a sudden police presence, a frightening escalation, and the sound of heavy footsteps nearby as officers closed in. What stayed with him most was not a single image alone but the combination of feeling trapped, hearing those footsteps, and realizing that the situation was out of his control. Even months later, when he tried to describe it, he found himself unable to finish the story cleanly, as if the memory itself pulled him off course. At times, he said, the event felt more real and vivid than ordinary memories, so that speaking about it could make him feel as though he were back there again. He also noticed that when the memory came on, he sometimes heard in his head the sounds he had heard during the frightening event, which made the whole scene come back with a force he found hard to dismiss.

In the weeks that followed, Jamal began organizing his life around the fear that he might be noticed, singled out, or caught off guard again. He started wearing concealing clothing, choosing outfits that helped him blend in rather than stand out, because he felt safer if people were less likely to pay attention to him. This was not limited to public settings; it shaped his mornings before work, when he stood in front of the mirror deciding what would draw the least notice. He also stopped going to unfamiliar places unless he could first picture exactly where he would be and how he would get out. As a journalist, this affected him directly. Assignments that once would have excited him now felt risky if they required him to enter neighborhoods, buildings, or events he had not already mentally mapped. He said he could not assess the danger in a new place, and that uncertainty made him reluctant to go at all. Over time, this had narrowed both his reporting and his daily routines, leaving him feeling less capable in the very work that had once given him a sense of purpose.

Jamal also described a pattern of checking behind him, especially when he was walking outside or moving through a hallway or station. Footsteps nearby were particularly difficult; when he heard someone behind him or even close enough that he could not tell who it was, he would turn his head again and again to see whether he was being followed. That vigilance happened in ordinary moments, not only in obviously threatening ones. He also found himself struggling to concentrate, especially while reading, planning stories, or listening to others. In a job that depended on attention, this left him frustrated and embarrassed, though he tried to hide it.

Certain songs had become unexpectedly loaded for him. He described hearing one in a store and feeling himself thrown back into the emotional landscape of the trauma and the losses that followed it. Anything that reminded him of someone he had lost, even indirectly, became something he tried to avoid. He admitted that he had also started avoiding anything that could bring up strong feelings of any kind, whether negative or positive, because he feared the intensity of what might surface if he let himself feel too much. That effort to stay emotionally flat had left him more distant from his partner and more withdrawn in daily life, though he did not describe it as a choice so much as a way of keeping himself from being overwhelmed.

By the time he sought help, Jamal was exhausted by living in a state of constant alertness and by the sense that his life had been permanently altered. What brought him in was the recognition that he could no longer keep functioning as he wanted to in his relationship or in his career without feeling on edge, distracted, and cut off from himself. What frightened him most was the possibility that this was now permanent and that he would never again feel like the capable, happy person he believed he had been before.
